On `r format(as.Date(min(search_log$date)), "%d %B %Y")` the `r nrow(oa)` searches of OpenAlex retrieved `r format(sum(oa$retrieved), big.mark = ",")` records on title and abstract, and the same searches of library-science, the author's store of sources verified against CrossRef, retrieved `r sum(search_log$retrieved[search_log$strand == "library-science"])`. `r if (all(!is.na(s2$error))) "Semantic Scholar refused every search made without an access key, so it contributed no records." else paste0("Semantic Scholar retrieved ", format(sum(s2$retrieved), big.mark = ","), " records.")` Once records sharing a DOI or a title were merged, and `r sum(records$routes == "grey")` guidelines, standards, inventory reports and methodological notes sought by hand from the IPCC, Environment and Climate Change Canada, Architecture for REDD+ Transactions and FAO were added, `r format(nrow(records), big.mark = ",")` unique records remained to be screened. Scopus and Web of Science were not searched, because both require an institutional key.

The author screened the first `r sum(records$screener == "author")` records on title and abstract, including a record when it mentioned natural, anthropogenic, human-induced or any other kind of disturbance. His decisions showed that a record was excluded when disturbance was only background to another subject, and the remaining `r format(sum(records$screener == "model"), big.mark = ",")` records were screened against a written form of the rule that said so, by a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) that read each title and abstract and was given his decisions as worked examples. Tried blind on `r validation$n` of his records, with the other `r sum(records$screener == "author") - validation$n` given as examples, the model agreed with him on `r validation$agree` [Cohen's κ = `r sprintf("%.2f", validation$kappa)`]. Of the `r format(nrow(records), big.mark = ",")` records, `r sum(records$decision == "include")` were included and `r sum(records$decision == "exclude")` excluded, `r sum(records$reason == "wrong-concept", na.rm = TRUE)` of them because they concerned forest or land but none of the concepts the questions turn on, and `r sum(records$decision == "undecided")` were left undecided because they had no abstract and their titles could not settle them. The full texts of the included and undecided records were sought from the open copies that OpenAlex lists, and `r sum(stringr::str_detect(works$status, "^(held|downloaded)"))` of the `r nrow(works)` works were held already or downloaded.

Each of the `r format(nrow(charting), big.mark = ",")` distinct works among the included and undecided records was then charted from its title and abstract by the same model under a written rule, which recorded the review questions the work bore on, the place and scale it studied, its main method, the disturbance it concerned, what it found, and a passage of its abstract, copied word for word, that supported the finding. Every passage was checked by script against the abstract it came from, and the `r sum(charting$basis == "title")` works with no abstract were charted from their titles alone. The charted works bore on the effect of the separation on reported emissions in `r on("q1")` cases, on the statistics of disturbance regimes in `r on("q2")`, on the uncertainty of carbon flux estimates in `r on("q3")`, on fire emission data and methods in `r on("q4")` and on crediting, buffers or reversal in `r on("q5")`, and `r sum(charting$role == "central")` of them bore directly on the subject of this study. The works were charted without their full texts, so a statement that the charted works contained no study of a given kind rests on titles and abstracts.

## Data sources

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Datasets this study read, with the release used and what each one supplies."
#| echo: true

sources <- data.frame(
  Dataset = c("FAOSTAT Emissions from Fires (GI)",
              "FAO AllFires_OrganicSoils table",
              "MODIS MCD64A1 Collection 6.1",
              "MODIS MCD12Q1 Collection 6.1"),
  Publisher = c("FAO", "FAO", "NASA", "NASA"),
  Supplies = c("Burned area, burned biomass and emissions by country and year",
               "Organic soil fire values set to zero in the published domain",
               "Monthly burned area at 500 m, the input FAOSTAT aggregates",
               "Annual land cover at 500 m, the vegetation strata FAOSTAT applies"),
  Period = c("1990-2024", "1990-2021", "2000-2024", "2001-2023"))
readr::write_csv(sources, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-sources.csv")
fmt_tbl(sources)
```

## Fire emissions from FAOSTAT

FAOSTAT computed each country's fire emissions as the burned area of a pixel multiplied by the fuel biomass consumption of its vegetation type and then by the default emission factor of that gas, aggregated to the country through the FAO Global Administrative Unit Layers, and disseminated the result for forest fires, savanna fires and fires in organic soils [@fao2025fires]. The methodological note stated that forest fire carbon dioxide was left out of the domain because it was counted in the FAOSTAT Forests domain, and that savanna fire carbon dioxide was left out on the assumption that regrowth balanced it within a year [@fao2025fires]. The domain nonetheless returned carbon dioxide for forest fires from 2001 onwards, and those are the values reported here. They were compared year by year with the value Canada submitted for the same item, which FAOSTAT carried in the same domain, as the ratio of the two, following the comparisons of FAOSTAT with national inventories by @grassi2022carbon and @nyawira2024pantropical and of an independent model with the inventories of European countries by @pilli2016modellinga.

The domain was retrieved through the FAOSTAT application programming interface, which required an account. The analysis chunk at the head of this document authenticated with the credentials stored in the environment, requested the domain for Canada and cached the response, so that a later render read the cached file rather than the service.


## Fires in organic soils

The values FAO withheld from the published domain were read from the `AllFires_OrganicSoils` table, which FAO released as a related document of the domain. The analysis chunk extracted every record from that document, keeping only lines that held a complete record so that a line broken across a page boundary could not enter the table as a partial one, and checked that the result held one record for every combination of area, year and reported element.


## The natural disturbance rule

Australia's rule was applied to the Canadian series in the form its inventory used, a year counting as natural when its fire emissions exceeded the mean of a baseline period by two standard deviations [@bowman2023wildfire]. The rule was run three times, on baselines of 13, 20 and 30 years, so that the effect of the baseline length could be read from the same data. The 13 year baseline was the length Australia itself used, 2000 to 2012.


## Canada's reported components

Canada's own disaggregated series was taken from Table 6-1 of the 2026 national inventory report, which Environment and Climate Change Canada published for every inventory year from 1990 to 2024 and for each province and territory separately [@eccc2026nir]. The table gave the net emissions of the land use sector, which is the account Canada reports, and on a separate line the net emissions of land affected by natural disturbance, which Canada tracks but leaves out of its reported total. Both lines were read for Canada and for British Columbia. Both were produced by Canada's National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System, whose core model, CBM-CFS3, grew each stand along an empirical yield curve and moved its carbon through a disturbance matrix for each type of disturbance, and whose two components summed to the net emissions and removals of the managed forest [@kurz2018quantifying]. Its fire matrices assumed that every fire burned at high severity [@thompson2026incorporating]. The share of the area burned in Canada that fell in British Columbia each year was computed from the Canadian National Fire Database, which stores the fire polygons of every provincial, territorial and federal agency in one archive. The two accounts were first compared over the whole inventory period, 1990 to 2024, by the mean and standard deviation of their annual net emissions, following the comparison of reported series under two partitions of the managed forest by @kurz2024revised, before the crediting arithmetic below was applied to the years from 2012.


## Crediting under the standard

The two deductions the standard applied were implemented as written, so that the share of gross reductions and removals a jurisdiction kept could be read off any uncertainty level. The uncertainty deduction took the adjustment factor of the standard's Equation 11 and the buffer took the contribution of its Table 2 [@art2021trees].


The uncertainty of each account was drawn from the published uncertainty of the model that produced Canada's estimates, a 95 per cent interval 32.2 Tg of carbon a year wide, taken here as a standard deviation applied to every annual flux in both accounts, which assumed the model was no more certain about a megafire year than about a quiet one [@metsaranta2017uncertainty]. The crediting level of the standard was the emissions of a five year historical reference period divided by five, and reductions in a year were that level minus the emissions reported for the year [@art2021trees]. Both were computed twice, once on the human activity component alone, which was the disaggregated account Canada reported, and once on the sum of the two components, which was the account a jurisdiction would have reported without the disaggregation. The reference period was 2012 to 2016 and the crediting period 2017 to 2024.


# Results

## Reported national emissions

```{r}
#| label: fig-accounts
#| fig-cap: "Net emissions of the land use sector for Canada and British Columbia, 1990 to 2024, in the account Canada reports, with natural disturbance separated, and in the undisaggregated account, the reported total plus the natural disturbance component. Positive values are emissions and negative values are removals."
#| echo: true

eccc |>
  dplyr::mutate(region = factor(dplyr::if_else(region == "BC", "British Columbia", region), levels = c("Canada", "British Columbia"))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(human, net), names_to = "account", values_to = "mt") |>
  dplyr::mutate(account = dplyr::if_else(account == "human", "Disaggregated, as reported", "Undisaggregated")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(year, mt, linetype = account)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Net emissions (Mt CO"[2]*"e)"), linetype = NULL) +
  th +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Separating natural disturbance cut the standard deviation of Canada's annual land use emissions from `r round(stats::sd(national$net))` to `r round(stats::sd(national$human))` Mt CO~2~e over 1990 to 2024, a factor of `r round(stats::sd(national$net) / stats::sd(national$human), 1)` (@fig-accounts). The account Canada reports averaged `r msd(national$human)`, while the same land without the separation averaged `r msd(national$net)`, the difference being the natural disturbance component, which ran from `r round(min(national$natural))` Mt in `r national$year[which.min(national$natural)]` to `r format(round(max(national$natural)), big.mark = ",")` Mt in `r national$year[which.max(national$natural)]`. In 2023 Canada reported `r national$human[national$year == 2023]` Mt where the undisaggregated account showed `r format(round(national$net[national$year == 2023]), big.mark = ",")` Mt. British Columbia's reported account averaged `r msd(province$human)` against `r msd(province$net)` without the separation, a standard deviation `r round(stats::sd(province$net) / stats::sd(province$human), 1)` times larger, and in 2023 the province reported `r province$human[province$year == 2023]` Mt against `r round(province$net[province$year == 2023])` Mt.

## Fire emissions in Canada

```{r}
#| label: tbl-canada-forest
#| tbl-cap: "Carbon dioxide from forest fires in Canada as FAOSTAT computes it at Tier 1, with the burned area it was derived from. The series begins in 2001 because that is the first year of the MODIS burned area input."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(forest, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-canada-forest.csv")
fmt_tbl(forest)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-canada-forest
#| fig-cap: "Carbon dioxide from forest fires in Canada, 2001 to 2024, as computed by FAOSTAT at Tier 1 from MODIS burned area."
#| echo: true

ggplot2::ggplot(forest, ggplot2::aes(Year, `CO2 (kt)` / 1000)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = expression(CO[2]~"(Mt)")) +
  th
```

Forest fires in Canada released `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / 1000), big.mark = ",")` Mt of carbon dioxide in 2023 on the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate, `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / mean(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year < 2023]), 1)` times the mean of the years before it and `r round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2023] / forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2020], 0)` times the quietest year of the series, 2020, at `r format(round(forest[["CO2 (kt)"]][forest$Year == 2020] / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1)` Mt (@fig-canada-forest).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-source-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Carbon dioxide from fires in other forest in Canada, as FAOSTAT computes it at Tier 1 and as Canada reported it to the UNFCCC, for the years both are available. FAOSTAT carries the reported series inside the same domain."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(gap, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-source-gap.csv")
fmt_tbl(gap)
```

The two sources disagree by more than they agree. Across the `r nrow(gap)` years in which both are reported, the FAOSTAT Tier 1 estimate is a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada itself submitted, running from `r min(gap$Ratio)` times in `r gap$Year[which.min(gap$Ratio)]` to `r max(gap$Ratio)` times in `r gap$Year[which.max(gap$Ratio)]` (@tbl-source-gap).

## Classifying a fire year as natural

```{r}
#| label: tbl-baselines
#| tbl-cap: "The natural disturbance threshold applied to Canadian forest fire emissions under three baseline lengths. The threshold is the baseline mean plus two standard deviations, and the years listed are those the rule classifies as natural."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(baselines, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-baselines.csv")
fmt_tbl(baselines)
```

The baseline length moved the threshold without moving the classification. Lengthening the baseline from 13 to 20 years raised the threshold from `r format(baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1], big.mark = ",")` to `r format(baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2], big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide, a rise of `r round(100 * (baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2] / baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1] - 1))` per cent, and both lengths classified the same `r length(strsplit(baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1], ", ")[[1]])` years as natural, `r baselines[["Years classified natural"]][1]` (@tbl-baselines). The 30 year baseline could not be run at all, because the FAOSTAT series covers only `r nrow(forest_co2)` years derived from observations, 2001 to 2024, and the years before that are filled rather than measured.

## Crediting with and without the separation

```{r}
#| label: tbl-credits
#| tbl-cap: "Emissions and reductions for Canada's managed land under the two accounts, 2017 to 2024, on a 2012 to 2016 reference period. The disaggregated account is the human activity component Canada reports; the undisaggregated account is the sum of the human activity and natural disturbance components. A negative reduction is emissions above the crediting level, which the standard treats as a reversal."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(credits, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-credits.csv")
fmt_tbl(credits)
```


The separation decides whether there is anything to credit. On the account Canada reports, reductions were positive in `r sum(split_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` crediting years and summed to `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent, with `r sum(!split_pos)` years below the crediting level, `r credits$Year[!split_pos][1]` at `r credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][!split_pos][1]` Mt and `r credits$Year[!split_pos][2]` at `r credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][!split_pos][2]` Mt. On the same land without the separation, reductions were positive in only `r sum(whole_pos)` years, and the shortfall in `r credits$Year[worst]` alone reached `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt, which is `r round(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]) / sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]))` times every reduction the disaggregated account earned across the whole period (@tbl-credits).

Neither deduction is reached in that case, because there is nothing to deduct from. The standard's reversal rule retires buffer credits equal to the lower of the emissions above the crediting level or every credit the jurisdiction has been issued, so an undisaggregated account of this land exhausts its buffer in `r credits$Year[which(!whole_pos)[1]]` and again in each later year that emissions exceed the level [@art2021trees].

## Crediting in British Columbia

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bc
#| tbl-cap: "Emissions and reductions for British Columbia under the two accounts, 2017 to 2024, on a 2012 to 2016 reference period. Both components are the provincial figures of the national inventory, and the burned area share is the province's share of the area burned in Canada."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(bc_credits, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-bc.csv")
fmt_tbl(bc_credits)
```


British Columbia followed the national pattern and more sharply. The province took `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2018]` per cent of the area burned in Canada in 2018 and `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent in 2023. On the disaggregated account its reductions were positive in `r sum(bc_split_pos)` of the `r nrow(bc_credits)` crediting years, summing to `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent. Without the separation they were positive in `r sum(bc_whole_pos)` years, and `r bc_credits$Year[bc_worst]` fell `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt below the crediting level (@tbl-bc).

## The uncertainty of each account

```{r}
#| label: tbl-uncertainty
#| tbl-cap: "Reductions and their uncertainty for Canada under the two accounts, from 10,000 Monte Carlo draws using the annual flux uncertainty published for Canada's forest carbon model. The interval is the 90 per cent interval the standard requires, its half width expressed against the mean reduction of the same draws, and the deduction is what the standard's adjustment factor takes from it. A percentage is printed only where the mean reduction is positive, since a percentage of a shortfall carries no meaning, and the undisaggregated deduction is therefore not reported."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(uncertainty, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-uncertainty.csv")
fmt_tbl(uncertainty)
```

Canada's own uncertainty analysis of the model behind these numbers reports a 95 per cent interval `r round(32.2 * 44 / 12)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent wide around a median of `r round(-0.8 * 44 / 12, 1)` Mt, and states plainly that "the CI for NBP cannot be meaningfully expressed in percentage terms because its range of possible values contains zero" [@metsaranta2017uncertainty]. Carried into the crediting arithmetic, that interval is wider than the reductions it qualifies. Across the `r sum(!is.na(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]]))` crediting years with a positive mean reduction, the interval of the disaggregated account ran from `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated interval (% of mean)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent of its own mean reduction, and the uncertainty deduction it implies is `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent (@tbl-uncertainty). The separation rescues the sign of the account and leaves the credit uncertain by more than its own size, which the disaggregation does not address.

## What survives the deductions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kept
#| tbl-cap: "The share of gross reductions and removals a jurisdiction keeps under the standard, by the reported uncertainty. The uncertainty deduction follows Equation 11 and the buffer follows Table 2 of the standard. The last column is the worst case in the five years after a reversal, when the buffer rises by five percentage points."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(deductions, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-kept.csv")
fmt_tbl(deductions)
```


The two deductions together are linear in the reported uncertainty, so the level at which a jurisdiction keeps nothing can be solved rather than searched. On the default buffer that level is an uncertainty of `r round(100 * break_even())` per cent, with all three mitigating factors and the smallest buffer the standard allows it is `r round(100 * break_even("1,2,3"))` per cent, and in the five years after a reversal it is `r round(100 * break_even(after_reversal = TRUE))` per cent. Below those levels the loss is still severe. At an uncertainty of 100 per cent the jurisdiction keeps `r deductions[["Kept, 25% buffer (%)"]][deductions[[1]] == 100]` per cent of its gross reductions and removals on the default buffer, and at 150 per cent it keeps `r deductions[["Kept, 25% buffer (%)"]][deductions[[1]] == 150]` per cent (@tbl-kept). Uncertainty of that size is not hypothetical, since the uncertainty chapter's own worked example prints ±150 per cent for one land category [@paciornik2019uncertainties].

## Fires in organic soils

```{r}
#| label: tbl-canada-peat
#| tbl-cap: "Burned area and emissions from fires in organic soils in Canada, as FAO computed them and then set them to zero in the published Emissions from Fires domain. Values for 1990 to 1995 are the average of the reconstructed series rather than observations, which is why they do not vary."
#| echo: true

readr::write_csv(canada, "03.outputs/TBL/tbl-canada-peat.csv")
fmt_tbl(canada)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-canada-peat
#| fig-cap: "Burned area of fires in organic soils in Canada, 1990 to 2021, from the FAO table that the published domain replaces with zeros. The flat section to 1995 is the filled part of the series and the rest is derived from satellite observations."
#| echo: true

ggplot2::ggplot(canada, ggplot2::aes(Year, `Burned area (ha)` / 1000)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Burned area (thousand ha)") +
  th
```


Over the `r nrow(obs)` years the satellite record covers, 2001 to 2021, fires in organic soils in Canada burned a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares a year and released a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide and `r format(round(mean(obs[["CH4 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of methane, none of which appears in the FAOSTAT domain a government downloads. The largest single year was `r obs$Year[which.max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]`, at `r format(round(max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares and `r format(round(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]][which.max(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide, and the smallest was `r obs$Year[which.min(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])]`, at `r format(round(min(obs[["Burned area (ha)"]])), big.mark = ",")` hectares.

The six years from 1990 to 1995 repeat one value, `r format(round(fill), big.mark = ",")` hectares, and that value is the mean of every year that follows them to the last digit the table prints, `r format(round(mean(post[["Burned area (ha)"]]), 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2)` hectares for 1996 to 2021 against `r format(round(fill, 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2)`. The filled years are therefore the average of the whole remaining series rather than of the window the methodological note describes, and any mean taken over the full series returns that same value whatever the observations do.

# Discussion

On the components Canada published in its 2026 inventory for 2017 to 2024, separating natural disturbance from human activity decided whether an account existed to credit, and it did not make that account precise. The managed land of the country reported reductions in `r sum(split_pos)` of the `r nrow(credits)` years, totalling `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent, while the same land accounted without the separation reported them in `r sum(whole_pos)` years and fell `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short of its crediting level in 2023 alone. British Columbia, with `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent of the area burned in Canada that year, reversed in the same way at the provincial scale, reporting `r round(sum(bc_credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_split_pos]), 1)` Mt separated against a shortfall of `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt unseparated. The separation was therefore not an adjustment to a reported number but the condition on which a jurisdictional credit existed at all. Earlier work had found the same dependence in reporting, since natural disturbance was among the reasons Canada did not elect forest management under the Kyoto Protocol [@kurz2008risk], revising the harvest record behind the partition moved the reported human sink by 113 Mt CO~2~e in 1990 [@kurz2024revised], and the treatment of wildfire as natural stood between a forestry source of 90.8 Mt CO~2~e a year and a reported sink of 4.7 Mt CO~2~e a year over 2005 to 2021 [@bysouth2024high]. In each case the partition rather than the forest moved the reported balance, and a standard that took the reported balance as its input carried the partition straight into the credit.

The rest of this Discussion took in turn the three places where the separation depended on choices the guidance left open, which were the uncertainty of a net near zero, the record behind the test of what was natural together with the period of regrowth, and the method that produced the fire emissions, and then compared the buffers of the standards before setting out the changes that would close these gaps and the limits of the study.

The separated account kept part of its reductions in only `r sum(banked > 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(banked))` years with a positive reduction, for a reason that was arithmetic rather than ecological. A percentage uncertainty was an interval divided by a reported value, so an account whose emissions and removals nearly cancelled reported an uncertainty far larger than either side of it, and @paciornik2019uncertainties warned against interpreting such a result "in cases where the point estimate is very small when compared with the size of the confidence interval". @metsaranta2017uncertainty met the same limit from the other direction, reporting an interval `r round(32.2 * 44 / 12)` Mt wide around a median of `r round(-0.8 * 44 / 12, 1)` Mt, and Canada's own inventory met it in its latest year, printing the 95 per cent interval of the carbon dioxide of Forest Land in 2024, a net of −1.9 Mt with an interval of −63 to 19 Mt, as 3,100 and −1,100 per cent [@eccc2026nir]. Applied to the crediting equations, the published interval produced uncertainty deductions of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent, larger than the reduction they were taken from in `r sum(over, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(over))` years with a positive reduction and smaller only in `r paste(uncertainty$Year[which(!over)], collapse = " and ")`, so the separation moved the reported quantity away from zero in the years the fires dominated and left it near zero in the years they did not. In `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]` it kept `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of its reduction, after the uncertainty deduction and a buffer that the shortfall of `r min(credits$Year[!split_pos])` had raised to `r 100 * trees_buffer(after_reversal = TRUE)` per cent. Regional carbon budgets elsewhere sat near zero within their uncertainty in the same way, in Australia [@haverd2013australian], in the Brazilian Amazon [@rosan2023contemporary] and in California, where the data could not establish whether the land was a source or a sink [@divittorio2021quantifying]. The standards differed in what such an interval cost. The adjustment factor of ART TREES rose with the half width of the interval without limit [@art2021trees], whereas the uncertainty set-aside of the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility stopped at 15 per cent for any aggregate uncertainty above 100 per cent [@fcpf2024buffer], so that under its rules a positive reduction kept at least `r round(100 * (1 - 0.15) * (1 - 0.40))` per cent of itself after both set-asides, whatever its uncertainty.

The length of the record behind the separation mattered less to the classification than to the threshold. Lengthening the baseline from 13 to 20 years raised the threshold that marked a year as natural by `r round(100 * (baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][2] / baselines[["Threshold (kt)"]][1] - 1))` per cent and marked the same five years, so the classification was insensitive to the choice while the threshold was not, and a 30 year baseline could not be tested because the satellite record behind the emissions covered only `r nrow(forest_co2)` years. The fire regime literature found the threshold sensitive in the same way at longer scales, with Weibull parameters that changed substantially between 22 and 31 years of record [@oliveira2011fire] and estimates of the fire cycle degraded by short-term variation in fire activity [@cyr2016quantifying]. Fire cycles estimated for Canada ran from 50 to 769 years [@johnson1991climatically; @arsenault2016unravelling], so a baseline of 13 to 30 years sampled a small part of one cycle, which was why the fire history literature turned to centuries of tree rings and millennia of charcoal wherever recent fires were too few to describe the historical range of variability [@gavin2007forest], and the closest analogue in that literature to an inventory baseline was the 26-year fire normal proposed for Yosemite [@lutz2011fire]. Of the three crediting documents read for this study, only Verra's tool set a record length, scoring natural risk over the last 100 years and allowing extrapolation from no fewer than 20 [@verra2024nprt]. Canada applied no baseline of any length, reconstructing instead the cause of every stand for the century from 1889 to 1989 and then reporting each burned area in the natural category for the 60 to 100 years it took to grow back to the age at which it could be logged [@kurz2024revised], while Australia tested fire seasons against a thirteen year mean [@bowman2023wildfire] and the worked European example built its series over the twenty years before the base year and assumed twenty years of regrowth [@ogle2019generic]. Three implementations used three temporal designs under guidance that specified none, which left the regrowth half of the account undefined. That half also carried the error of the model, since CBM-CFS3 underestimated the net biomass gain of undisturbed boreal stands by 10 per cent over 71 years [@bernier2010reconstructing], and it was that regrowth which returned to the human account when a burned stand crossed the age threshold.

The fire emissions inside both accounts came from one method. Canada's fire matrices assumed high severity throughout, and a sub-model built on mapped burn severity gave regional emissions typically 10 to 25 per cent lower [@thompson2026incorporating], so both accounts in this study carried that difference, and the account without the separation carried nearly all of it, because Canada placed every wildfire in the natural component [@eccc2026nir]. The comparison of sources showed that the Tier 1 estimate published by FAOSTAT ran a median of `r round(median(gap$Ratio), 1)` times the value Canada submitted for the same item, which placed the choice of source on the same scale as the choice of method. Differences of that size were common wherever independent fire estimates were compared, from a fivefold spread among satellite burned area datasets for Siberia [@kukavskaya2013fire] to a twofold difference for France in 2022 between an estimate constrained by atmospheric measurements and the global GFAS estimate [@vallet2025soil], and FAOSTAT's estimate of the global land sector differed in sign from what countries reported [@grassi2022carbon]. The same database set Canada's organic soil fire emissions to zero while computing them at a mean of `r format(round(mean(obs[["CO2 (kt)"]])), big.mark = ",")` kilotonnes of carbon dioxide a year over the satellite record, so a government checking its inventory against that source checked it against a figure the publisher did not stand behind outside Southeast Asia [@fao2025fires].

The buffers the standards withheld against reversal did not follow the fire regime of the land they covered. ART TREES applied 25 per cent to every jurisdiction unless three mitigating factors were met [@art2021trees], the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility added 0 to 5 percentage points for exposure to natural disturbance within a set-aside of 10 to 40 per cent [@fcpf2024buffer], and only Verra's tool scored the history of events in the area itself, for projects rather than jurisdictions [@verra2024nprt]. The fire cycles charted for Canada ran from 50 to 769 years between regions [@johnson1991climatically; @belisle2011fire; @arsenault2016unravelling], the global analysis of reversal risk placed North American conifer forests among those at greatest risk [@wu2026global], and British Columbia, which took `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2018]` per cent of the area burned in Canada in 2018 and `r bc_credits[["Burned area share (%)"]][bc_credits$Year == 2023]` per cent in 2023, fell `r format(abs(bc_credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][bc_worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt short of its crediting level on the unseparated account. A buffer set as one percentage for Canada as a whole would therefore have applied the same reserve to regions whose fire cycles differed by more than a factor of ten, an argument for buffer contributions set from regional fire regime statistics, as the contributions prepared for the carbon removals regulation of the European Union were set from modelled regional loss to disturbance [@marinelli2026risk].

Crediting standards inherited the silence of the guidance directly, because the REDD+ Environmental Excellence Standard permitted the exclusion of natural disturbance on the authority of the guidance and pointed to the chapter that defined the term without defining how far back the record must reach [@art2025trees3; @ogle2019generic], and both of the standard's deductions were then taken from whatever remained. A standard that credited jurisdictions therefore rested on a boundary it did not set and could not audit, since two jurisdictions applying the same clause to the same fire record could report different natural shares according to how far back their labelling reached and how long their regrowth periods ran. Four changes would close that gap, which were to specify the length of the record behind any natural disturbance test rather than leave it to the participant, to state the regrowth period over which later removals were disaggregated together with the evidence for it, to compute the uncertainty deduction on gross emissions and gross removals rather than on a net that approached zero, so that a jurisdiction was not penalised for the arithmetic of cancellation rather than for the quality of its data, and to set the buffer contribution from the fire regime of the region it covered rather than as one percentage for every jurisdiction.

Two limits qualified these results. The uncertainty analysis applied one published interval to every annual flux in both accounts, which assumed the model was no more certain about a quiet year than about a megafire year. Both accounts also used Canada's figures as reported, so the study compared two ways of summing the output of one model, whose fire matrices assumed high severity throughout [@thompson2026incorporating], rather than two independent estimates of the fires, and FAOSTAT was the only independent estimate in it.

# Conclusions

Two accounts of the same Canadian managed land, one separating natural disturbance from human activity and one not, were run through the crediting level, the uncertainty deduction and the buffer withholding of the REDD+ Environmental Excellence Standard for the fire years 2017 to 2024, and the separation decided whether any reduction existed to credit, `r round(sum(credits[["Disaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][split_pos]), 1)` Mt of carbon dioxide equivalent separated against a shortfall of `r format(abs(credits[["Undisaggregated reductions (Mt)"]][worst]), big.mark = ",")` Mt in 2023 alone unseparated, which meant that a jurisdiction in a megafire regime could report a creditable balance only by excluding the fires, on guidance that set no length for the record the exclusion rested on. The separated account remained uncertain by more than its own size, with an uncertainty deduction of `r format(min(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(uncertainty[["Disaggregated deduction (%)"]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` per cent, and kept part of its reductions only in `r mc_split$Year[which(banked > 0)]`, `r round(banked[which(banked > 0)], 1)` per cent of them, so separation alone left little to issue.

The literature this study reviewed had treated the separation in national reporting since the Kyoto period [@canadell2007factoring; @kurz2018quantifying] and the statistics of fire regimes since at least 1978 [@wagner1978class], and it had compared inventories with independent estimates [@pilli2016modellinga; @grassi2022carbon] and mapped the risk of reversal [@wu2026global], but no work it charted had carried a jurisdiction's account through a crediting standard both with and without the separation. The standards that relied on the separation needed to specify the record length, state the regrowth period, take the uncertainty deduction from gross emissions and gross removals rather than from a net that approached zero, and set their buffers from the fire regime of each region, and the code and data behind every number here were published so that a national government could repeat the comparison on its own inventory.
